title: Pascal's wager
examples: What is the many gods objection?
Can you choose to believe in God?

explain.say: Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician of the 1600s who helped invent probability theory. He thought reason alone could not prove whether God exists, so he asked a different question: is it wise to bet on God?

Pascal said we cannot avoid the bet, so look at the four possibilities. If you believe and God exists, you gain everything. If you believe and there is no God, you lose a little. If you don't believe and God exists, you lose everything.

items: Your choice | If God exists | If God does not exist
Don't believe | Infinite loss | Small gain

explain.say: Since an infinite gain outweighs any small cost, even if the chance of God is small, Pascal concluded that the sensible bet is to believe. It is an early example of what we now call decision theory.

items: Reason can't settle whether God exists
But we must choose how to live
Infinite gain outweighs a small cost
So the wise bet is to believe

draw.text: Pascal's notes were published after his death as the Pensées, in 1670.

explain.say: Critics raise objections. Which God should you bet on, when religions disagree? Can you really choose to believe something, like flipping a switch? And would God reward belief chosen only out of self-interest?

items: Many gods: which one should you bet on?
Belief is not a switch you can flip
A God might not reward belief from self-interest
Infinite stakes make the maths strange

explain.say: Pascal's answer to the second objection was practical: if you cannot yet believe, live as believers do, pray and join in worship, and belief may grow. Supporters add that the wager was meant to start someone searching, not to replace faith.

a: Faith from fear isn't real faith
b: Act as believers do and belief can grow
The wager starts a search, not faith itself

explain.say: Pascal himself knew that belief is not only a calculation. One of his most famous lines says that the heart has its reasons which reason does not know.

draw.value: The heart has its reasons which reason does not know.
draw.label: Pascal, Pensées

faq.a: Pascal's wager is an argument by the 17th-century French thinker Blaise Pascal. He said we cannot prove whether God exists, but we must live one way or the other. If you believe and God exists, you gain infinitely; if you believe and God does not exist, you lose little. So, he argued, the wise bet is to believe.

Blaise Pascal, who lived from 1623 to 1662, was a French mathematician, scientist and Christian thinker. He helped found probability theory, built one of the first calculating machines, and studied air pressure. His notes on faith were published after his death as the Pensées.

faq.q: What is the many gods objection?
faq.a: The many gods objection says that the wager does not tell you which God to bet on. Many religions describe different gods with different demands, so believing in one might still be the wrong bet. Pascal was thinking of the Christian God, but the wager alone cannot choose between faiths.
asks: which God should you bet on

faq.q: Can you choose to believe in God?
faq.a: Most philosophers think you cannot simply decide to believe something, the way you decide to raise your hand. Pascal agreed, and suggested people who wished to believe should live as believers do, praying and joining in worship, so that belief might grow over time.
asks: can you force yourself to believe

faq.q: Would God reward someone who believes just to win the bet?
faq.a: Critics ask whether a good God would value belief chosen only to gain a reward or avoid punishment. Some suggest God might prefer honest doubters. Supporters reply that the wager is a first step, and that sincere faith can grow from it.

faq.q: What are the main objections to Pascal's wager?
faq.a: The main objections are: it does not say which God to bet on; belief cannot simply be chosen; a God might not reward self-interested belief; the costs of religious life may not be small; and using infinite rewards makes the probability maths behave strangely.
asks: what is wrong with Pascal's wager

faq.q: Is Pascal's wager an argument that God exists?
faq.a: No. It does not try to prove God exists. It is an argument about what is wise to believe when the evidence seems unclear, based on comparing the possible gains and losses.
asks: what kind of argument is the wager

faq.a: Expected value is a way of judging a bet by multiplying each possible result by how likely it is and adding them up. Pascal's wager uses this idea: an infinite reward multiplied by even a small chance still gives an infinite expected value, which outweighs any finite cost.
asks: what is expected value in the wager

faq.a: The Pensées, French for thoughts, are Pascal's notes for a book defending the Christian faith. He died before finishing it, and the notes were published in 1670. The wager appears in them, along with reflections on faith, doubt and the human condition.

faq.q: What does the heart has its reasons mean?
faq.a: This famous line from Pascal's Pensées means that some of our deepest convictions, like love or faith, come from the heart and intuition rather than from logic alone. It shows Pascal did not think belief was only a calculation.

faq.q: What would an atheist say about Pascal's wager?
faq.a: Many atheists reply that you cannot honestly believe something just because it would pay off, that the wager could be used for any god, and that a religious life has real costs. Some also say an honest God would respect a sincere search for truth more than a bet.
asks: non religious view of the wager
why do non-believers reject the wager

faq.q: Is Pascal's wager still discussed today?
faq.a: Yes. Philosophers still debate it, and it is studied as an early example of decision theory, the mathematics of choosing under uncertainty. Its structure, weighing a small cost against a huge possible outcome, also appears in modern debates about risk.

facts: Blaise Pascal lived from 1623 to 1662 and was a French mathematician and Christian thinker.
Pascal's wager appears in the Pensées, his notes published after his death in 1670.
Pascal helped found probability theory, through letters with Pierre de Fermat.
The many gods objection says the wager cannot tell you which god to bet on.
Pascal suggested that people who wished to believe should live as believers do, so that belief might grow.

quiz.say: Recall. In Pascal's wager, what do you gain if you believe and God exists?
quiz.show: Believe, and God exists: what do you gain?
quiz.why: Pascal said belief, if God exists, brings an infinite reward, which is why it outweighs any small cost.

wrong.0: A small gain is what Pascal said non-believers get if God does not exist.
wrong.1: Pascal said believers gain the most, not nothing, if God exists.

quiz.say: Apply. Someone says, but what if the true God is from another religion entirely? Which objection is this?
quiz.show: What if the true God is a different one? Which objection?
quiz.why: The many gods objection says the wager does not tell you which of many possible gods to bet on.

wrong.1: The problem of evil asks why a good God allows suffering.
wrong.2: The Euthyphro dilemma asks whether good depends on God's commands.
wrong.3: The first cause objection asks what caused God, about a different argument.

quiz.say: Think. Pascal suggested that a person who cannot believe should pray and join in worship. Which objection was he answering?
quiz.show: Pray and join in worship: answering which objection?

options.show: That belief cannot simply be chosen
options.say: That belief cannot simply be chosen

options.show: That the universe has no cause
options.say: That the universe has no cause

quiz.why: Pascal knew belief is not a switch, so he suggested habits of faith could help belief grow over time.

wrong.1: That objection belongs to the first cause argument, not the wager.
wrong.2: The existence of evil is the problem of evil, a separate debate.
